aspects.says: Reflective lookups are cached, and MethodHandles serve performance-critical calls.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
aspects.reason: practised in 41-reflection 10.3.4 (metadata-cache, method-cache, method-handles); the speed itself cannot be graded deterministically

aspects.says: Circular dependencies overflow a naive injector, and reflectively injected fields need happens-before ordering.
aspects.reason: cycles are practised in 41-reflection 10.3.3 (mini-container) and happens-before in modules 17 and 18

aspects.says: A standard processor can only generate new files; it cannot modify the source it inspects (Lombok does so through javac internals).
java.lang.reflect.Proxy proxies interfaces only; classes need CGLIB or Byte Buddy.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
aspects.reason: a limit of the JDK API rather than a choice the reader's code makes; every proxy practice in this section proxies an interface

aspects.says: A container calls @PostConstruct methods after creating a bean and @PreDestroy methods before discarding it.
Reading a Class<?> element from Element.getAnnotation() throws MirroredTypeException; read it through AnnotationMirror or the exception's TypeMirror.
aspects.reason: an API detail the page mentions in one sentence without an example; the processor practice keeps to the page's own generate-and-report example

aspects.says: Under the module system setAccessible on another module's private members needs an opens directive.
aspects.reason: needs a multi-module build; every practice runs on the class path, where the rule does not apply

aspects.says: toString, equals and hashCode reach the InvocationHandler too and need explicit handling.
aspects.reason: practised in 41-reflection 10.3.3 (tracing-proxy), whose edge cases grade exactly this

aspects.says: A compile-time processor extends AbstractProcessor, names its annotations with @SupportedAnnotationTypes and its version with @SupportedSourceVersion, and generates files through the Filer.
A processor reports problems through the Messager, and an ERROR diagnostic fails the compilation.
Proxy.newProxyInstance builds a class at run time that implements the given interfaces and sends every call to handler.invoke.
Processing runs in rounds: files generated in round N are processed in round N+1, and a final round with processingOver() true follows.
Runtime processing reads RUNTIME annotations through reflection; a simple injector sets each @Inject field from a registry, keyed by the annotation's value or else the field's name.
Runtime processing costs reflection and startup time; compile-time generation costs build time but nothing at run time.
aspects.reason: a performance trade-off that no deterministic test can observe

aspects.says: A dynamic proxy and an InvocationHandler add method-level security: the handler reads @RequiresPermission from the implementation's method and refuses the call before it runs.
Processors are registered with javac through META-INF/services.
aspects.reason: a build-configuration fact; the practice's tests hand the processor to javac directly, and nothing in a service file can be graded apart from the build

aspects.says: Reflection reaches private members only after setAccessible(true).
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: Method.invoke wraps the target's exception in InvocationTargetException; the handler rethrows its cause, or a proxy's caller gets UndeclaredThrowableException.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: Annotations are validated at startup, not during request processing, with error messages that say what is wrong.
